nameStory: The Arctic fritillary gets its name from its love of cold, northern climates - it's one of the few butterflies that thrives in the chilly conditions near the Arctic Circle. The word 'fritillary' comes from the Latin word for dice-box, referring to the checkered pattern on many species' wings that resembles the spotted markings on old gaming dice.
description: The Arctic fritillary is a small, orange-brown butterfly with intricate black markings that create a beautiful checkered pattern across its wings. This hardy little flier typically has a wingspan of about 1.5 to 2 inches, making it smaller than many of its fritillary cousins. Its wings have a slightly worn, weathered look that helps it blend into the rugged northern landscapes where it lives. You'll notice distinctive silvery spots on the undersides of its hindwings that catch the light when it lands.

idTips.label: Wing pattern
idTips.description: Orange-brown wings with black checkered markings that feel papery to the touch when viewed up close, creating an intricate mosaic pattern

idTips.label: Underwing spots
idTips.description: Distinctive silvery-white spots on the underside of hindwings that gleam like tiny mirrors in sunlight

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small butterfly with wingspan around 1.5-2 inches, noticeably smaller than a Monarch but larger than a Pearl Crescent

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Low, somewhat erratic flight close to the ground with quick, fluttering wingbeats followed by brief glides

idTips.label: Wing texture
idTips.description: Wings appear slightly weathered or faded, with a matte finish rather than the glossy sheen of some other butterflies

habitat: In New England, Arctic fritillaries are found in cool, moist areas at higher elevations, particularly in the northern mountains of Vermont, New Hampshire, and Maine. Look for them in alpine meadows, bog edges, and openings in coniferous forests where their host plants - various violets - grow in acidic, peaty soils. They prefer areas that stay cool even in summer, often near streams or in spots that catch morning dew.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active, but you might find overwintering caterpillars on violet leaves if you search carefully in their preferred cool habitats.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight time occurs from mid-June through August, when adults are most active on sunny days between 10 AM and 3 PM, nectaring on wildflowers.
seasonality.fall: Adults have finished flying by early September, but newly hatched caterpillars may be found feeding on violet leaves before winter.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity; caterpillars overwinter in a dormant state, hidden among leaf litter and low vegetation.

funFact: Arctic fritillaries are so adapted to cold weather that they can actually fly in temperatures that would ground most other butterflies - they've been observed flying actively when it's only 50°F outside, thanks to their ability to vibrate their flight muscles to generate body heat!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Bog Fritillary, which shares similar habitats and size. Remember: Arctic fritillaries have more pronounced silvery spots underneath and tend to look more 'weathered' or faded on top, while Bog Fritillaries appear fresher and more vibrant orange.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Arctic,' these butterflies don't actually live at the North Pole - the name refers to their preference for the cold conditions found in northern regions and high elevations. They're also sometimes called 'purplish fritillary' due to a subtle purple sheen visible on their wings in certain lighting.
compareHints: Compared to other Boloria fritillaries in New England, the Arctic fritillary is the most cold-adapted and northern in distribution. It's smaller than the American Silver-bordered Fritillary and has more muted colors than the brighter Meadow Fritillary. Unlike the Bog Fritillary which prefers wet meadows, Arctic fritillaries are more likely to be found in rocky, mountainous terrain at higher elevations.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Boloria relatives in New England, the American Silver-bordered Fritillary is distinguished by its prominent silver hindwing spots, while the Meadow Fritillary lacks silver markings entirely.
Among its Boloria relatives in New England, the meadow fritillary is the most widespread and the one you're most likely to encounter in typical meadow habitats.
